report.verdict: Chile in late-2026 is two markets moving in opposite directions: a mature, SCJ-regulated land-based casino sector shrinking in real terms (9M-26 GGR CLP 401.9bn / ~$395m, -7.9% real for the 22 concession casinos; visits -11%) and a large, wholly unlicensed online market that the courts, Subtel and the tax authority are now squeezing (79 domains DNS-blocked since September; 19% VAT levied on offshore gaming margin with no licence attached). The Senate Economy Committee voted 3-1 on 9 Nov 2026 to replace the government's licensing bill with a ban or a Polla/Lotería monopoly, while the Kast government counters with a 22%-of-GGR licence regime and a total advertising and bonus ban; the choice between those two paths, due to start being resolved at the committee vote on 1 Dec 2026, is the single swing factor for any entrant.

summary: **A two-speed market with no regulated online channel.** Land-based casinos are the only licensed casino gaming in Chile: 25 venues (22 concessions under Ley 19.995 plus 3 municipal) produced GGR ("ingresos brutos del juego"/win, gross of tax) of CLP 549.3bn (~$540m) in FY-2025 and CLP 401.9bn (~$395m) in 9M-2026 (SCJ). Online betting and casino are entirely unlicensed; no regulator publishes an online GGR figure and press estimates of ">US$650m a year" are unverified and almost certainly a stakes/turnover-type number rather than GGR.

**Land-based volumes are eroding in real terms.** The 22 Ley 19.995 casinos booked CLP 372.8bn (~$366m) GGR in 9M-26, -7.9% real (-3.9% nominal vs CLP 388.1bn in 9M-25); the 3 municipal casinos CLP 29.2bn (~$29m), -5.9% real. Visits fell 11.25% to 4.07m while spend per visit rose 3.8% real to CLP 91,639 (~$90) — fewer, higher-value customers. Diario Financiero's August 2026 review put the seven-year decline at ~20% of revenue and ~30% of visits.

**Casino tax take is falling faster than GGR.** Taxes devengados by the 22 concession casinos were CLP 141.3bn (~$139m) in 9M-26 (-8.5% real): specific gaming tax CLP 61.7bn (~$61m, 20% of GGR net of VAT, split 50/50 regional governments/municipalities), VAT CLP 59.5bn (~$58m), entry tax CLP 20.1bn (~$20m, 0.07 UTM ≈ CLP 5,071/~$5 per visit). FY-25 taxes were CLP 194.2bn (~$191m), -4.7% real; effective burden ≈38% of GGR. On top, concession 'oferta económica' bid payments ran CLP 69.0bn (~$68m) in 2025 and CLP 54.4bn (~$53m) in 9M-26.

**The online bill (Boletín 14.838-03) is in its fifth year.** Introduced March 2022; approved by the Chamber 12 Dec 2023; Senate Economy Committee in general 2 Apr 2024 (unanimous); Senate floor in general 13 Aug 2025 (27-3-5); >570 amendments filed by mid-2026; a technical working group produced 'five axes' in Sept 2026 (platform control, user protection, ad limits, strict tax regime, blocking); article-by-article debate opened 27 Oct 2026; the Economy Committee has scheduled its vote for Tuesday 1 Dec 2026.

**The Senate committee has backed prohibition, not licensing (9 Nov 2026, 3-1-1).** Two amendments were approved: Ibáñez (FA)/Saavedra (PS) — ban on operating, offering or advertising online betting in Chile, with prison terms (up to 15 years per iGB) and carve-outs for state lotteries, authorised racetracks and land-based casinos; and Núñez (RN, Senate President)/Gatica (RN) — no private market, online reserved to Polla Chilena de Beneficencia and Lotería de Concepción, with court-ordered shutdowns. The texts are to be merged, then go to the Finance Committee, the Senate floor and back to the Chamber (third reading) — a cross-party ban coalition spanning RN to the Frente Amplio.

**The Kast government still wants a licensed market — at 22% of GGR.** Finance Minister Jorge Quiroz backs a 22% tax on operators' gaming revenue, up from the Senate general text's 20% of gross gaming income + 19% VAT + a 1% responsible-gambling levy; Senator Walker wants 'a much higher rate'; Senator Sánchez's conditions are a cap on licences, access controls, high taxes and ad limits. Whether land-based casinos may go online splits the pro-regulation camp (Walker for, Ossandón against).

**The government's own amendments (27 Oct 2026) are among the strictest in LatAm.** Total ban on online-betting advertising — licensed or not — extending to agencies and media; ban on bonuses and promotions even outside advertising; mandatory biometric identity verification; default deposit and time limits set at account opening (tightening immediate, loosening only after 72h and re-confirmation); mandatory risk detection with forced pauses/suspensions; a single national self-exclusion register. Illegal advertising becomes a crime (presidio menor, mínimo a medio, plus 10–20 UTM ≈ CLP 0.72–1.45m / ~$712–1,424), aggravated if aimed at minors. The industry body aPAL objects that a total ad ban stops players distinguishing licensed from illegal sites.

**Enforcement has moved from theory to DNS blocking.** The Supreme Court (rol 18.080-2025, 30 Sep 2025, on protection actions by Lotería de Concepción and Polla) held online betting sites operate illegally and ordered ISPs to block them; in April 2026 it reversed an Appeals Court finding that blocking had been complied with; on 8 Aug 2026 the Santiago Court of Appeals set a permanent DNS-blocking procedure with lists validated by the SCJ. Subtel then ordered Entel, Movistar, Claro, GTD, WOM and VTR to block 42 domains (1 Sep 2026) and 37 more (21 Sep 2026) within 48 hours — covering Betano, Coolbet, JugaBet, 1xBet, Betsson, Rojabet, Betsala, MiCasino, Estelarbet, Betcris, KTO, Marathonbet, Betway, Betfair, Bet365 and Sporting Bet — with successive lists for mirrors promised.

**Taxed but not licensed: the SII now collects 19% VAT on offshore gaming margin.** SII Resolución Exenta N°69 (2 Jun 2026) opened the simplified non-resident digital-services VAT regime to online betting/casino operators; Ordinario N°1658 (8 Jul 2026) set the taxable base on the gaming margin (GGR); a list of 25 registered platforms was published 15 Jul 2026 and had grown to 39 by Sept 2026. The SII insists this 'does not validate the activity in any way' (8 Sep 2026) — operators therefore pay VAT on GGR, remain illegal, and are being blocked at the same time.

**Land-based incumbents are fighting the SII regime in court.** The Asociación Chilena de Casinos y Juegos (16 casinos, ~67% of venues) filed an amparo económico at the Santiago Court of Appeals (reported 21 Nov 2026) arguing the SII has 'organised the taxation of an activity prohibited by law', that the margin-based VAT base has no statutory footing, and that registered platforms use the nómina to resist blocking; it seeks annulment, withdrawal of the list and an interim order. Contraloría declined to rule (dictamen D348/2026, 10 Jul 2026).

**Online operator landscape — concentrated visibility, weak apps.** GR8 Tech's Operator Lens: Chile (Oct/Nov 2026) finds Betano, JugaBet and Coolbet hold 86% of online visibility among analysed brands; JugaBet leads organic search in both betting and casino terms; ~70% of traffic to key gambling sites is mobile yet few apps are well positioned; Instagram is the largest social channel; 1xBet leads live coverage at 846 events/hour (esports, virtuals, minor leagues); operators list 8,935 slots on average but only 11% of the 597 most-promoted titles appear at more than one operator.

**Leaked Curaçao filings give the only hard online unit economics.** Latamwin (W&C N.V.): 2024 gaming revenue before bonuses CLP 39.1bn (~$38m), +24.6% on CLP 31.4bn (~$31m); bonuses CLP 9.8bn (25% of gross); payment-processing costs CLP 9.2bn (~$9m, 24% of gross); marketing/affiliates CLP 2.6bn (~$2.6m); net profit CLP 11.2bn (~$11m). Estelarbet Chile 2024: stakes US$113.3m, deposits US$17.8m (6.4x recycling), GGR US$5.8m (5.1% hold; US$5.1m casino, US$0.7m sports), NGR US$4.1m, EBITDA US$1.1m, 6,437 daily actives. Rojabet (Media Entertainment N.V.) sales fell from US$46.2m (2023) to US$30.8m (2025) with losses each year; Betsala grew to €3.3m (2024), targeting €9.9m for 2026.

**Payments are card/bank-transfer rails, not mobile money — and they are expensive.** Chile has no M-Pesa-type ecosystem; grey operators rely on card acquiring, bank transfers and local PSP/wallet aggregators, which cost Latamwin ~24% of gross gaming revenue in 2024 — a drag that a licensed regime with mainstream acquiring would largely remove, but which the blocking campaign and any payment-blocking powers would worsen. The SCJ and Sernac warned on 24 Nov 2026 that prizes on blocked sites may go unpaid with no recourse.

**State operators are the political centre of gravity.** Polla Chilena de Beneficencia (state-owned; its Xperto product is the only legal online sports betting) and Lotería de Concepción (Universidad de Concepción) brought the blocking litigation, report mirror sites to the court, and would receive an online monopoly under the Núñez/Gatica amendment. Horse-racing (Teletrak) and the lotteries are exempted in the ban text. FY-2025 lottery sales were not retrievable in this research (n/a).

**Political direction: regulate-with-restrictions versus prohibit.** The Kast administration (in office since 11 Mar 2026) is pro-licensing but withdrew the bill's urgency on 22 Oct 2026 (oficio 192-374; 'sin urgencia' as of 14 Nov), while the Senate's cross-party ban bloc, the state lotteries and the land-based casino lobby (which is itself barred from going online) all push the other way. A separate Chamber initiative seeks to restrict the taxation of online betting (i.e., stop the SII de facto regularisation) [details unverified].

**Macro/FX headwind.** The peso is at its weakest since July 2022 — BCCh observado CLP 1,017.66 on 24 Nov 2026, spot above CLP 1,030 after a 3.9–5.9% copper slump — so USD-reported casino revenue is falling faster than CLP figures suggest (Yogonet's 9M-26 USD 444.7m used a ~905 rate; at today's rate the same CLP is ~$395m).

**Read-through for B2Tech: do not launch into the grey market now; build a licence-ready position.** Operating today means DNS blocking, 19% VAT with no rights, criminal exposure, and — critically — losing eligibility for the bill's transitional licences, reserved for applicants that have not operated illegally in Chile in the prior 12 months. The value play is a clean, Chile-domiciled licence applicant (or B2B platform partner to local casinos/lotteries if they are let online), modelled at 22–25% of GGR + 19% VAT + 1% RG levy with zero advertising and zero bonuses — a retention-, SEO- and app-led economics, where GR8 Tech's data says incumbents are weakest (apps, local SEO, differentiated content).

**Base case (our estimate): no licensed private market before 2H-2027.** We assign ~40% to a prolonged stalemate (bill stalls; de facto prohibition via blocking + VAT), ~35% to a licensed regime enacted by end-2027 with ≥22% GGR tax, a total ad ban and a capped number of licences, and ~25% to a statutory ban/state monopoly. Land-based GGR should finish 2026 at roughly CLP 530–540bn (~$520–530m, -2% to -4% nominal; estimate), with blocking offering only marginal relief.

segments.name: Land-based casinos (SCJ-regulated)
segments.headline: Only licensed casino gaming in Chile; 9M-26 GGR CLP 401.9bn (~$395m), -7.9% real, visits -11%, tax take -8.5% real — a mature market in structural decline, barred from going online.
narrative: The Superintendencia de Casinos de Juego (SCJ), created by Ley 19.995, regulates 22 concession casinos plus three legacy municipal-concession venues. Its Q3-2026 release (3 Nov 2026) shows the 22 concession casinos generated gross gaming income (win, before tax) of CLP 372,774m (~$366m) in the first nine months of 2026, a 7.9% real decline on the same period of 2025 (CLP 388,096m, ~$381m; -3.9% nominal). The three municipal casinos added CLP 29,163m (~$29m), -5.9% real, taking the system to roughly CLP 401.9bn (~$395m); Yogonet's read of the SCJ Boletín Estadístico gives CLP 402,759m — the difference is immaterial but note Yogonet mis-signed the 22-casino change as +7.9% while the regulator's own release says -7.9% real. Full-year 2025 was CLP 509,826m (~$501m) for the concession casinos and CLP 39,483m (~$39m) for the municipal venues, CLP 549.3bn (~$540m) in total, against more than CLP 554bn (~$544m) in 2024 — broadly flat nominal, roughly -4% real.

The volume picture is weaker than the revenue picture. The 22 concession casinos recorded 4,067,872 visits in 9M-26, down 11.25% year on year, while average spend per visit rose 3.8% in real terms to CLP 91,639 (~$90), from CLP 86,019 (~$85) for FY-25 and CLP 87,649 (~$86) at H1-26. The sector is therefore living off a smaller, more intensive customer base rather than growing its funnel; Diario Financiero's August 2026 'radiografía' of the physical gaming industry put the seven-year decline at about 20% of revenue and almost 30% of visits. Monthly run-rates in 2026 have been CLP 48,049m (~$47m) in January, 44,257m (~$43m) in February, 45,491m (~$45m) in April, 47,553m (~$47m) in May and 42,473m (~$42m) in June — i.e. a CLP 42–48bn (~$42–47m) monthly band with no sign of acceleration. In January–February 2026 the largest venue, Dreams' Monticello (Santiago), produced CLP 20,110m (~$20m), 21.8% of system win, followed by Enjoy Viña del Mar at CLP 9,994m (~$10m); Dreams and Enjoy are the two dominant groups.

Taxation is heavy and falling faster than revenue. Taxes devengados by the concession casinos were CLP 141,329m (~$139m) in 9M-26, -8.46% real, split into the specific gaming tax of CLP 61,688m (~$61m; 20% of GGR net of VAT, distributed 50% to regional governments and 50% to municipalities), VAT of CLP 59,519m (~$58m; 19%) and the entry tax of CLP 20,123m (~$20m; 0.07 UTM per entry — CLP 5,071 / ~$5 at the November UTM of CLP 72,440). FY-25 taxes were CLP 194,214m (~$191m), -4.7% real, after more than CLP 196bn (~$193m) in 2024; the effective burden is ~38% of GGR before the 'oferta económica' — the concession bid payments casinos committed in the licensing rounds — which added CLP 69,042m (~$68m) in 2025 and CLP 54,374m (~$53m) in 9M-26. Including bid payments, the state's take exceeds half of concession-casino GGR, which explains why the industry's political priority is protection from online substitution rather than expansion.

Commercially, the land-based sector is both a potential partner and an obstacle. Concession casinos are expressly not allowed to offer online gaming (Senator Walker: 'hoy día no pueden hacerlo'), and the Asociación Chilena de Casinos y Juegos (16 casinos, ~67% of venues) has gone to court against the SII's VAT registration of offshore operators, arguing it amounts to a de facto regularisation of an illegal activity. The casino lobby is thus aligned with the prohibition bloc in the Senate unless the bill grants casinos online rights — the point on which pro-regulation senators are split (Walker for, Ossandón against, citing a 'legal monopoly' risk). For a platform provider, the strategic question is whether the eventual law routes online rights through existing concession holders (making casinos the natural B2B customers) or through a separate licence class open to new entrants; the Chamber-approved text envisaged a separate licence with SCJ renamed 'Superintendencia de Casinos, Apuestas y Juegos de Azar'.

segments.name: Online betting & casino (unlicensed / offshore)
segments.headline: Large, growing and illegal: three brands own 86% of visibility, leaked filings show double-digit growth and 24%-of-GGR payment costs, and since September 2026 the state is DNS-blocking and VAT-taxing operators simultaneously.
narrative: There is no regulated online gambling in Chile and therefore no official measure of its size; the only legal online products are the state lotteries' (Polla's Xperto sports betting, Lotería online draws) and horse-racing tote. Under the Supreme Court's September 2025 ruling (rol 18.080-2025), privately operated online betting and casino sites — all offshore-licensed, mostly Curaçao and Malta — operate illegally. Market-size claims circulate without a basis: the figure repeated in the press of 'more than US$650 million a year' is not attributed to any regulator and, judged against the operator-level data below, looks like a stakes or deposits number rather than GGR; we treat it as unverified. Our own working estimate, built up from the leaked filings and the three dominant brands' relative scale, is online GGR in the US$250–400m range for 2025 — i.e. half to three-quarters of land-based GGR — and should be labelled an estimate.

The competitive structure is concentrated at the top and fragmented below. GR8 Tech's Operator Lens: Chile (published late Oct 2026, promoted 24 Nov 2026) finds that Betano, JugaBet and Coolbet together account for 86% of online visibility among the operators analysed; JugaBet, a locally focused brand, outranks the internationals in organic search on both betting and casino keywords; ~70% of traffic to key gambling sites is mobile yet relatively few operators have strong app positions; Instagram is the largest social audience in most cases; 1xBet leads live coverage with an average 846 events per hour, driven by esports, virtuals and minor competitions; and the average casino lobby carries 8,935 slots while only 11% of the 597 most-promoted titles appear at more than one operator — a signal that content curation, not catalogue size, differentiates. These are visibility and product metrics from a B2B supplier's research, not revenue shares, and should be read as such.

The Curaçao Papers leak (reported by Chócale and BioBio, Sept 2026) is the only hard window into unit economics. W&C N.V. (Latamwin) declared 2024 net gaming revenue before bonuses of CLP 39,083m (~$38m), +24.6% on CLP 31,357m (~$31m) in 2023; bonuses of CLP 9,796m (25% of gross), leaving CLP 29,287m (~$29m) of operating revenue; payment-processor costs of CLP 9,225m (~$9m, 24% of gross / 31% of net); marketing and affiliates of CLP 2,625m (~$2.6m); and a draft net profit of CLP 11,164m (~$11m) — a ~38% net margin that explains why operators have tolerated legal risk. Estelarbet's Chilean business plan showed 2024 stakes of US$113.3m on deposits of US$17.8m (6.4x recycling), GGR of US$5.8m (a 5.1% hold, US$5.1m casino and only US$0.7m sports), NGR of US$4.1m after bonuses, EBITDA of US$1.1m and 6,437 daily active players, with marketing budgeted to rise from US$0.41m to US$1.4m in 2025. Not everyone is growing: Media Entertainment N.V. (Rojabet) saw sales fall from US$46.2m (2023) to US$34.2m (2024) and US$30.8m (2025), sports revenue halving to US$12.5m, with net losses in each year; Betsala grew from €0.54m (2022) to €3.3m (2024) with targets of €5.6m (2025) and €9.9m (2026). The pattern — casino-led hold, heavy bonusing, expensive payments, share consolidating toward the big three — is typical of a grey market about to be regulated or closed.

Enforcement changed decisively in 2026. After the Supreme Court in April reversed the Santiago Court of Appeals' view that ISPs had complied with the 2025 blocking order, the Appeals Court on 8 Aug 2026 fixed a permanent procedure: DNS blocking of specifically identified domains validated by the SCJ, with ISPs reporting execution to the court. Subtel ordered the six ISPs (Entel, Movistar, Claro, GTD, WOM, VTR) to block 42 domains on 1 Sep 2026 and 37 mirrors/sub-domains on 21 Sep 2026, each within 48 hours, covering Betano, Coolbet, JugaBet, 1xBet, Betsson, Rojabet, Betsala, MiCasino, Estelarbet, Betcris, KTO, Marathonbet, Betway, Betfair, Bet365 and Sporting Bet, and stated the process will continue for new mirrors; Polla has committed to report mirrors. In parallel, the SII's Res. Ex. 69 (2 Jun 2026) and Ord. 1658 (8 Jul 2026) brought offshore operators into the non-resident digital-services VAT regime on a gaming-margin base: 25 platforms registered by 15 Jul 2026, 39 by September. The outcome is the worst of both worlds for an operator — 19% VAT on GGR with no licence, DNS blocking, criminal exposure for advertising under the pending amendments, and the SCJ/Sernac publicly warning players (24 Nov 2026) that winnings on blocked sites may go unpaid.

For B2Tech the implication is clear: entering the grey market now would (i) incur VAT at 19% of GGR plus ~24% payment friction with no legal protection, (ii) expose the brand to blocking and to the government's proposed criminalisation of advertising, and (iii) disqualify the company from the bill's transitional licences, which the Finance Ministry's summary reserves for applicants that have not operated illegally in Chile in the preceding 12 months and that meet technical standards of comparable jurisdictions and solvency tests. The opportunity, if a licence regime emerges, lies precisely where GR8 Tech's data shows incumbents are weak — native apps, Chile-specific SEO, differentiated content — under rules that will likely prohibit advertising and bonuses and thereby neutralise the incumbents' main acquisition weapons.

Rojabet (Media Entertainment N.V.) sales fell from US$46.2m (2023) to US$34.2m (2024) and US$30.8m (2025), sports halving to US$12.5m, net losses each year; Betsala grew from €0.54m (2022) to €3.3m (2024), targeting €5.6m (2025) and €9.9m (2026).
Pattern — casino-led hold, heavy bonusing, expensive payments, share consolidating to the big three — is typical of a grey market about to be regulated or closed.

blocks.heading: Enforcement in 2026
blocks.takeaway: Since September 2026 the state is DNS-blocking and VAT-taxing offshore operators simultaneously — the worst of both worlds for an operator.
points: Supreme Court in April reversed the Santiago Court of Appeals; on 8 Aug 2026 the Appeals Court fixed permanent DNS blocking of SCJ-validated domains with ISPs reporting execution.
Subtel ordered six ISPs (Entel, Movistar, Claro, GTD, WOM, VTR) to block 42 domains on 1 Sep 2026 and 37 mirrors on 21 Sep 2026, each within 48 hours; Polla committed to report mirrors.
Blocked brands include Betano, Coolbet, JugaBet, 1xBet, Betsson, Rojabet, Betsala, MiCasino, Estelarbet, Betcris, KTO, Marathonbet, Betway, Betfair, Bet365 and Sporting Bet.
SII Res. Ex. 69 (2 Jun 2026) and Ord. 1658 (8 Jul 2026) put offshore operators in the non-resident digital-services VAT regime on a gaming-margin base: 25 registered by 15 Jul 2026, 39 by September.
Result: 19% VAT on GGR with no licence, DNS blocking, criminal exposure for advertising under pending amendments, and SCJ/Sernac warning (24 Nov 2026) that winnings on blocked sites may go unpaid.

blocks.heading: Implication for B2Tech
blocks.takeaway: Entering the grey market now would cost 19% VAT plus ~24% payment friction, expose the brand to blocking, and disqualify B2Tech from transitional licences.
points: Finance Ministry summary reserves transitional licences for applicants not operating illegally in Chile in the preceding 12 months, meeting comparable-jurisdiction technical standards and solvency tests.
Government proposes criminalisation of advertising, adding brand exposure.
Opportunity under a licence regime lies where incumbents are weak per GR8 Tech — native apps, Chile-specific SEO, differentiated content.
Rules will likely prohibit advertising and bonuses, neutralising incumbents' main acquisition weapons.

segments.name: Lottery, horse racing & state operators
segments.headline: Polla Chilena and Lotería de Concepción are the only legal online gambling and the plaintiffs behind the blocking regime; one Senate amendment would hand them the whole online market.
narrative: Chile's lottery and sports-pool rights sit with two statutory operators: Polla Chilena de Beneficencia, a state-owned company under the Finance Ministry whose Xperto product is the only legal online sports-betting offer in the country, and Lotería de Concepción, owned by the Universidad de Concepción, which sells draw games including online. Pari-mutuel horse-race betting through the hipódromos (Teletrak network) is likewise authorised, including online. FY-2025 sales and GGR for these entities were not retrievable within this research and are shown as n/a rather than estimated.

Their market relevance in 2026 is as much legal as commercial. Lotería de Concepción's and Polla's protection actions produced the Supreme Court's 30 Sep 2025 ruling that private online betting sites are illegal and must be blocked, the April 2026 reversal that forced ISPs back into compliance, and the 8 Aug 2026 Appeals Court procedure under which the SCJ validates domain lists for Subtel. Polla has publicly committed (3 Sep 2026) to report mirror sites, making the state lotteries the de facto enforcement arm. Politically, Senate President Paulina Núñez's amendment (approved in committee 9 Nov 2026) would reserve online gambling to Polla and Lotería outright, and the Ibáñez/Saavedra ban text exempts state lotteries, authorised racetracks and land-based casinos from the prohibition.

For an operator or platform supplier, the lotteries represent two scenarios: in a monopoly outcome they are the only addressable customers for B2B sportsbook/casino technology (a tender-driven, low-margin but defensible route), while in a licensing outcome they are competitors with a statutory brand advantage and a track record of litigating against private entrants. Either way, Xperto's current scale is the best proxy for 'legal' online demand, and the absence of published 2025 figures is itself a data gap worth closing before any investment decision.

segments.name: Licensing & tax: current regime and the pending online bill
segments.headline: Casinos pay ~38% of GGR plus bid fees; online is taxed at 19% VAT with no licence; the bill offers 5-year licences at 20–22% of GGR with a clean-hands rule — but the Senate committee has voted for prohibition.
narrative: The existing framework is Ley 19.995 (2005), under which the SCJ grants casino concessions by competitive bid (the 'oferta económica'), with a statutory cap of 24 concessions nationally outside the legacy municipal casinos and 15-year terms [statutory details from the law, not re-verified in this research]. Operators pay a specific gaming tax of 20% on GGR net of VAT (50% to regional governments, 50% to municipalities), 19% VAT, and an entry tax of 0.07 UTM per visit (CLP 5,071 / ~$5 in Nov-26). On 9M-26 numbers the effective burden is 37.9% of GGR (CLP 141.3bn / ~$139m on CLP 372.8bn / ~$366m), before bid payments of CLP 54.4bn (~$53m). There is no online licence of any kind, and concession casinos are not permitted to operate online.

Online operators are nonetheless taxed. SII Resolución Exenta N°69 of 2 Jun 2026 extended the simplified VAT regime for non-resident digital-service providers to online betting, casino and games of chance, reversing the SII's own 2023 position that excluded them because the activity is illegal; Ordinario N°1658 of 8 Jul 2026 fixed the taxable base as the gaming margin (GGR). The SII published its list of 25 registered platforms on 15 Jul 2026 (39 by September) and, challenged, said on 8 Sep 2026 that collecting the tax 'does not validate the activity in any case'. The casino association's amparo económico (Santiago Court of Appeals, Nov 2026) attacks the resolution for applying a VAT taxable event designed for digital entertainment to gambling and for setting a margin base by administrative letter; Contraloría abstained (D348/2026). If the court sides with the casinos, the SII list disappears and the quasi-regularisation argument operators have used against blocking goes with it.

The bill — Boletín 14.838-03, 'Regula el desarrollo de plataformas de apuestas en línea' — as approved in general by the Senate (13 Aug 2025, 27-3-5) would: convert the SCJ into the Superintendencia de Casinos, Apuestas y Juegos de Azar with licensing and supervisory powers over online platforms; require operators to be companies registered and domiciled in Chile; issue general licences for five years; tax operators at 20% of gross gaming income plus 19% VAT plus a 1% levy for responsible gambling (a further earmark for sport was discussed in the Chamber text [unverified]); permit advertising only by licensed platforms (Art. 51); criminalise illegal gambling, with the law in force the first day of the month after publication for enforcement purposes and the licensing regime operative once the reglamento is issued (six months). Crucially, transitional licences would be available only to applicants that have not operated illegally in Chile in the prior 12 months and can show compliance with technical standards of comparable jurisdictions and solvency — a clean-hands rule that favours new entrants and B2B-backed local companies over today's grey incumbents.

The 2026 amendment war has pushed the text in two incompatible directions. The Kast government's indications (27 Oct 2026; Undersecretary Vallebona) retain licensing but ban all online-betting advertising — with or without licence, extending to agencies and intermediaries — ban bonuses and promotions, mandate biometric KYC, default deposit/time limits with a 72-hour loosening delay, risk-behaviour interventions and a single exclusion register, and make illegal advertising a crime (presidio menor mínimo a medio plus 10–20 UTM, CLP 0.72–1.45m / ~$712–1,424; aggravated if targeting minors); on 24 Nov 2026 Finance Minister Quiroz added a 22% tax on operators' gaming revenue. The Senate Economy Committee, by contrast, approved 3-1-1 on 9 Nov 2026 two prohibition amendments — Ibáñez/Saavedra (ban on operating, offering or advertising online betting in Chile regardless of server location, prison terms reported at up to 15 years, exemptions for lotteries, racetracks and casinos) and Núñez/Gatica (no private market, online reserved to Polla and Lotería, court-ordered shutdowns) — to be merged at the next session. Senator Sánchez's statement that the Executive 'did not want to take any' of the working group's proposals (licence cap, entry controls, high taxes, ad limits) 'and that is why the path of prohibition was taken' captures the dynamic: prohibition is partly a negotiating lever for a tougher licensing deal.

Procedurally, the merged committee text goes to the Senate Finance Committee, then the Senate floor, then back to the Chamber (which passed a licensing version in Dec 2023) for a third reading and possibly a mixed commission; the Executive withdrew urgency on 22 Oct 2026, so there is no statutory clock. The realistic tax envelope if licensing survives is 22–25% of GGR plus 19% VAT plus 1% RG — a total take of roughly 40–45% of GGR, comparable to the land-based burden and at the high end of LatAm (Brazil 12% GGR, Colombia 15% GGR + VAT on top, Peru 12% + 1% consumption levy) — with no advertising, no bonuses and a capped licence count. That is survivable for a low-CAC, product-led operator and hostile to bonus-driven acquisition models.

segments.name: Payments, advertising, responsible gambling & enforcement
segments.headline: Card and bank rails rather than mobile money, costing grey operators ~24% of GGR; advertising faces a total ban even for licensees; DNS blocking is live and expanding; RG rules in the pipeline are among LatAm's tightest.
narrative: Chile is a card- and bank-account economy, not a mobile-money market: deposits to offshore sites run through card acquiring, bank transfers and local PSP/wallet aggregators, and the Curaçao filings show how expensive those grey rails are — W&C N.V. (Latamwin) paid CLP 9,225m (~$9m) to payment processors in 2024, 23.6% of gross gaming revenue and 31.5% of post-bonus revenue, more than three times its marketing and affiliate spend of CLP 2,625m (~$2.6m). Bonuses consumed a further 25% of gross. Estelarbet's plan implies 6.4x deposit recycling (US$113.3m staked on US$17.8m deposited) and a 5.1% blended hold, consistent with a casino-led market. A licensed regime with mainstream acquiring would be the single largest margin lever available to a legal entrant; conversely, the 'five axes' agreed by the Senate working group in Sept 2026 include blocking of illegal operators, and payment-side blocking is a live option in the debate [specifics unverified].

Advertising is where the regulatory temperature is highest. Betting brands have been prominent sponsors in Chilean football and digital media (GR8 Tech ranks Instagram as the largest social channel for most operators), but the government's 27 Oct 2026 amendments would prohibit all online-betting advertising in Chile — explicitly including licensed operators — together with bonuses and promotions, with licence revocation for licensees and criminal penalties for unlicensed advertising (presidio menor, 10–20 UTM ≈ CLP 0.72–1.45m / ~$712–1,424; aggravated when imagery, language or channels target minors). The industry group aPAL argues a total ban prevents players from identifying licensed sites and will slow channelisation; senators' own amendments go further with scheduling and black-and-white format rules [per Infogate]. For planning purposes, B2Tech should assume zero above-the-line marketing and zero sign-up bonuses in any Chilean licence, which puts the weight on organic search (where local brand JugaBet already beats the internationals), app-store presence (where GR8 Tech finds few strong positions) and CRM.

Responsible-gambling design in the government text is prescriptive: biometric identity verification at onboarding; preventive deposit and session-time limits set by default at account opening, tightenable instantly but loosenable only after 72 hours and re-confirmation; mandatory detection of risk behaviour with forced pauses, deposit restrictions or temporary suspension; a national register of excluded persons that operators must check before opening accounts; a ludopatía fund financed by the 1% levy; and an absolute bar on minors. These are implementable with a modern PAM but add cost and friction, and they signal that the eventual regulator — an SCJ with no online experience — will lean on technical standards imported from comparable jurisdictions, which the transitional-licence test explicitly references.

Enforcement capacity has caught up with the law in 2026 and will not reverse whichever legislative path wins. The judiciary has established the illegality of offshore sites (Supreme Court, Sept 2025), forced ISP compliance (April 2026) and institutionalised DNS blocking with SCJ-validated lists (Aug 2026); Subtel executed two waves (42 and 37 domains) in September with 48-hour deadlines and has committed to rolling updates for mirrors; the SII has the registered operators' identities and margin data; and consumer-protection bodies (SCJ, Sernac) are warning players that winnings on blocked sites may be unrecoverable. The leakage channels that remain — VPNs, mirror domains, crypto on-ramps — are real but shrink the addressable grey market and raise its cost. A ban outcome would add criminal liability for operators, advertisers and intermediaries; a licensing outcome would add the clean-hands filter. In both, the value of having never operated in the grey market rises.

highlights.text: Demonstrated, growing demand: leaked 2024 accounts show Latamwin's Chilean gaming revenue up 24.6% to CLP 39.1bn (~$38m) with a ~38% net margin, and Estelarbet turning US$113m of stakes on just US$17.8m of deposits — a casino-led market with high recycling that a licensed entrant could serve at far lower payment and legal cost.

Incumbents are strong on visibility but weak where it is cheapest to compete: Betano/JugaBet/Coolbet hold 86% of visibility, yet ~70% of traffic is mobile and few operators have strong app positions, and only 11% of top-promoted slots overlap across lobbies — app, local-SEO and content-curation whitespace (GR8 Tech).

The bill's clean-hands transitional licence (no illegal operation in Chile in the prior 12 months, proven technical standards and solvency) structurally favours a new, B2B-backed, Chile-domiciled applicant over today's grey operators — a rare case where not being in the market is an asset.

The Executive is still on the licensing side and has put a concrete number on the table — 22% of GGR (24 Nov 2026) — within a total envelope (≈22–25% + 19% VAT + 1% RG) that is heavy but survivable for a low-CAC, retention-led model; advertising and bonus bans would neutralise the incumbents' main acquisition advantage.

Enforcement is now real and institutionalised (Supreme Court → permanent DNS procedure → 79 domains blocked in September; SII registration of 39 operators), so a future licensed market would start with meaningfully higher channelisation than Chile's grey past implies.

Land-based casinos (9M-26 GGR -7.9% real, visits -11%) are motivated partners for an online B2B platform if the final text lets concessionaires online — the Dreams/Enjoy duopoly and 22 concession venues are an addressable B2B base; the state lotteries are the fallback customer in a monopoly outcome.

lowlights.text: The Senate Economy Committee voted 3-1-1 on 9 Nov 2026 for prohibition (Ibáñez/Saavedra: full ban with prison terms up to 15 years; Núñez/Gatica: Polla/Lotería monopoly), with a cross-party bloc from RN to the Frente Amplio — a licensed private market is no longer the base case.

The government's own amendments ban all advertising (including by licensees) and all bonuses/promotions, criminalise illegal advertising (presidio menor + 10–20 UTM ≈ CLP 0.72–1.45m / ~$712–1,424) and impose biometric KYC and default limits — even the 'good' outcome is a no-marketing market.

Operating today means 19% VAT on gaming margin with no licence rights (SII Res. Ex. 69/2026), DNS blocking of 79 domains with rolling mirror updates, Sernac/SCJ warnings to players, and forfeiture of eligibility for transitional licences — the grey option is value-destructive.

No regulator data exists for online market size; the '>US$650m/yr' press figure is unverified and likely a stakes-type number — any business case rests on leaked operator filings and estimates (our estimate: US$250–400m GGR, 2025).

Timeline risk: the bill is in year five, carries no urgency (withdrawn 22 Oct 2026), faces a Finance Committee, a floor vote and a return to the Chamber; the casino association's amparo against the SII and Polla/Lotería litigation add further legal variables — 2027 enactment is far from assured.

Payments friction: grey rails cost Latamwin ~24% of gross GGR in 2024; a ban would add payment-blocking and criminal liability for intermediaries, and even a licensed regime will inherit heavy RG-driven KYC costs.

FX and macro: the peso at CLP 1,017.66 observado (24 Nov 2026) — spot above 1,030, weakest since July 2022 after a copper slump — erodes USD-denominated revenue; land-based GGR is already falling 7.9% real.

forecast.intro: The rule set in play has moved from the Senate's August-2025 general text (licensing by a renamed SCJ, 5-year licences, 20% GGR tax + 19% VAT + 1% RG levy, advertising permitted for licensees) to two mutually exclusive 2026 alternatives: the Kast government's October/November amendments (licensing at 22% of GGR with a total advertising and bonus ban, biometric KYC, default limits and a national exclusion register) and the Senate Economy Committee's 9 Nov 2026 prohibition amendments (no private market; Polla/Lotería monopoly; prison terms). The shift was driven by the Supreme Court's illegality finding, the state lotteries' litigation, the land-based casino lobby, and a cross-party political backlash over ludopatía and minors — not by any failure of demand. Meanwhile enforcement (DNS blocking, SII VAT registration) has already changed the operating reality irrespective of the bill.

forecast.view: Our independent view (all probabilities and figures are estimates): **~40% prolonged stalemate** — the merged ban text and the government's licensing text deadlock through the Finance Committee and floor, leaving de facto prohibition via blocking and VAT through 2027; **~35% a licensed private market enacted by end-2027**, with a tax of 22–25% of GGR plus VAT and the 1% levy (≈40–45% of GGR all-in), a total advertising and bonus ban, biometric KYC and a capped licence count, with first licences no earlier than 2028 given the six-month reglamento; **~25% a statutory ban or Polla/Lotería monopoly**. On market size, **online GGR of roughly US$250–400m in 2025 (estimate)** is our working figure; under licensing we would expect regulated GGR to reach only 50–60% of that in year one because of the no-ad/no-bonus regime and the clean-hands exclusion of incumbents, rising thereafter as blocking bites. **Land-based casino GGR should finish 2026 at ~CLP 530–540bn (~$520–530m), -2% to -4% nominal (estimate)**, with 2027 flat-to-down; the tax take will fall faster than GGR as visits decline. **Leverage direction for the state: tax burden on online is going up, not down** — the only live debate is between 22% and 'much higher'. For B2Tech, the right posture is licence-ready and grey-free: a Chile-domiciled vehicle, a local-casino or lottery B2B track, and a product plan built for zero-marketing economics; commit capital only on the Senate floor vote, not the committee.
watch: 1 Dec 2026: Senate Economy Committee vote on the merged ban text versus the government's 22% licensing package — and whether casinos are granted online rights (Walker vs Ossandón).
Senate Finance Committee treatment of the tax rate (22% vs 'much higher') and the 1% RG levy; whether the Executive restores urgency after withdrawing it on 22 Oct 2026.
Santiago Court of Appeals ruling on the casino association's amparo económico against SII Res. Ex. 69/2026 and the 39-operator nómina — a win for casinos removes the de facto registration shield.
Subtel/SCJ blocking cadence (next domain lists, mirror sites, any move to payment blocking) and observable traffic leakage via VPN/mirrors.
The Chamber's separate initiative to restrict taxation of online betting, and any third-reading dynamics if the Senate sends back a ban.
SCJ FY-2026 bulletin (expected Feb 2027): whether land-based GGR holds the CLP 530–540bn (~$520–530m) range and whether visits stabilise after blocking.
Polla Chilena's Xperto and Lotería online growth as the only legal online demand proxy; football sponsorship exits by blocked brands.
USD/CLP: a sustained move above 1,030 further compresses USD-reported revenue and raises the cost of imported platform/content.

report.confidenceNote: FX: USD/CLP 1,017.66 (Banco Central de Chile dólar observado, 24 Nov 2026); UTM Nov-2026 CLP 72,440. Land-based casino figures are regulator-reported (SCJ releases for FY-2025, H1-2026 and 9M-2026) — High confidence; note Yogonet mis-signed the 9M-26 concession-casino change as +7.9% whereas the SCJ release states -7.9% real, and Yogonet's USD conversions use period rates (~905), so differ from ours. Legislative status (bill history, 9 Nov committee vote, 27 Oct/24 Nov government amendments, Subtel blocking orders, SII resolutions) is as of 24 Nov 2026 — High. Online market size is NOT reported by any Chilean regulator; the '>US$650m/yr' press figure is unverified and our US$250–400m GGR figure is an estimate built from leaked Curaçao filings (draft accounts) and GR8 Tech visibility data — Low. Lottery/racing FY-2025 sales could not be retrieved (n/a). Items drawn from the statute/memory and not re-verified today are flagged [not re-verified]: 15-year concession term and 24-licence cap under Ley 19.995; the Chamber text's sports earmark; licence fee schedule. The GR8 Tech report itself is gated; its findings are taken from the publisher's summary (iGB, 24 Nov 2026) and the GR8 Tech landing page.
